source_text: Sed argumentabitur quilibet posse et duo summa magna consistere, distincta atque disiuncta in suis finibus, et utique aduocabit exemplum regna terrarum, tanta numero et tamen summa magna in suis quibusque regionibus, et putabit ubique humana diuinis conferenda. iam ergo si huic argumentationi locus dabitur, quid prohibet, non dico et tertium et quartum deum inducere, uerum tot iam numero quot et gentium reges? de deo agitur, cuius hoc principaliter proprium est, nullius exempli capere comparationem. hoc natura ipsa, si non aliquis Esaias, uel ipse per Esaiam deus, contionabitur: cui mesimilabitis? diuinis forsitan comparabuntur humana, deo non ita. aliud enim deus, aliud quae dei. denique qui exemplo uteris regis quasi summi magni, uide ne iam non possis eo uti. rei enim, etsi summum magnum est in suo solio usque ad deum, tamen infra deum; comparatus autem ad deum excidet iam de summo magno, translato in deum. hoc si ita, quomodo uteris eius rei exemplo ad dei comparationem quae, dum ad comparationem accedit, amittitur? quid nunc, si nec inter reges plurifarium uideri potest summum magnum, sed unicum et singulare, apud eum scilicet, qui rex regum ob summitatem magnitudinis et subiectionem ceterorum graduum quasi culmen dominationis excipitur\'? sed etiam [alterius formae] reges, qui singulares in unione imperii praesunt si(militer) minutalibus, ut ita dixerim, regnis, (si) undique conferantur in examinationem, qua constet, quis eorum praecellat in substantiis et uiribus regni, in unum necesse est summitas magnitudinis eliquetur, omnibus gradatim per comparationis exitum de magnitudinis summa expressis et exclusis. I adeo etsi in disperso multifarium uidetur summum magnum, suis uiribus et sua natura et suo statu unicum est. proinde cum duo dii conferuntur ut duo [reges et duo] summa magna, in alterum concedat necesse est unio summi magni ex sententia comparationis, quia summum uictoria sua constat, superato aemulo alio magno, non tamen summo, atque ex defectione, aemuli solitudinem quandam de singularitate praestantiae suae possidens unicum est. ineluctabilis iste complexus in hoc sententiam constringit: aut negandum deum esse summum magnum, quod nemo patietur sapiens, aut nulli alii communicandum.
pass_a_gloss: But someone will argue that it is possible for two great supreme beings to exist, distinct and separate within their own boundaries, and certainly he will cite the example of the kingdoms of the earth, so many in number and yet supreme in their respective regions, and he will think that human things are to be compared with divine things. Now therefore, if this argument is given a place, what prevents, I do not say introducing a third and fourth god, but as many as there are kings of nations? The question is about God, whose principal property is this, to not be taken in comparison with any example. This is by nature itself, if not some Isaiah, or God himself through Isaiah, will speak: to whom will you liken? Perhaps human things will be compared with divine things, but not with God. For God is one thing, and the things of God are another. Finally, whoever uses the example of a king as if supreme, see that you may not be able to use it. For the thing, although it is supreme in its own throne up to God, is nevertheless beneath God; but compared to God, it will already fall from being supreme, having been transferred to God. If this is so, how do you use the example of this thing for comparison with God, which, as soon as it approaches comparison, is lost? What now, if not even among kings can the supreme being be seen as multiple, but as unique and singular, namely with him who is the king of kings, because of the summit of greatness and the subjection of the other degrees, as it were, the culmination of domination? But also the kings of another form, who are singular in the union of empire, presiding over, as it were, minute kingdoms, if they are compared from all sides in an examination, by which it is established who among them excels in the substances and powers of the kingdom, it is necessary that the summit of greatness be filtered out, all the degrees being gradually expressed and excluded through the exit of comparison. Therefore, even if the supreme being seems multiple when dispersed, it is unique in its powers and its nature and its state. Accordingly, when two gods are compared as two supreme beings, it is necessary that the union of the supreme being concede to the other, according to the sentence of comparison, because the supreme being consists in its own victory, having overcome the other great being, not however supreme, and from the defeat, possessing a certain solitude of singularity of its excellence, it is unique. This inevitable complex constrains the sentence: either it must be denied that God is the supreme being, which no wise person will tolerate, or it must not be shared with anyone else.

bible_refs.note: Isaiah is mentioned as a possible speaker

pass_b_english: Someone will argue that two supreme beings can coexist, distinct and separate within their own boundaries. They will cite the example of earthly kingdoms, many in number yet each supreme in its own region, and they will think human things can be compared with divine things.

If that argument is allowed, what stops us from introducing not just a third and fourth god, but as many gods as there are kings of nations? The issue concerns God, whose defining property is that he admits no comparison with any example. Nature itself declares this — if not Isaiah, then God speaking through Isaiah: "To whom will you liken me?" (Isaiah 40:18). Human things may be compared with divine things, but not with God. For God is one thing; the things of God are another.

Finally, whoever uses a king as an example of a supreme being should see that the example collapses. A king may be supreme on his own throne up to God, yet he remains beneath God; once compared to God, he ceases to be supreme, having been transferred to God. If that is so, how can you use that thing as an analogy for God when the analogy vanishes the moment it approaches the comparison? What if even among kings the supreme is not multiple but unique and singular — namely the King of kings, who, by the summit of greatness and the subjection of all other ranks, stands as the culmination of dominion?

Even kings of another sort, singular in the union of empire and presiding over what we might call minute kingdoms, if examined from every side to determine who excels in the substance and power of their realms, will inevitably yield a single summit of greatness, all lower degrees gradually excluded by the process of comparison. Thus, even when the supreme appears multiple in dispersion, it is unique in its powers, nature, and state. Accordingly, when two gods are compared as two supreme beings, the union of the supreme must concede to the other by the verdict of comparison, because the supreme consists in its own victory — having overcome another great being, not supreme — and from that defeat it possesses a solitude of singular excellence, making it unique. This inescapable logic forces the conclusion: either deny that God is the supreme being, which no wise person will accept, or refuse to share that supremacy with anyone else.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex logical structure of the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source. The scripture reference in Pass B (Isaiah 40:18) is a correct identification of the allusion 'cui mesimilabitis?' (to whom will you liken [me]?) found in the Latin.
